body:
Multi-agent debate is sold on diverse viewpoints. At equal calls, a plain vote beat it.

In one replication on GSM8K that I reviewed (Huang et al., 2024), self-consistency with nine samples scored 88.2 percent. Debate with nine responses scored 83.0.

I wrote a paper auditing the published results that hold compute constant. The pattern is consistent: at matched cost, most of the reported gain from debate and persona schemes disappears, and a vote over the agents' independent first answers explains most of what remains.

The positive results are real, but they are not diversity results. The strongest one uses a single model in every role. The large agentic gains track whether the task decomposes. That is division of labour, not independent judgement.

"Multi-agent" names four different mechanisms: voting, synthesis by an aggregator, decomposition and viewpoint diversity. Matched-cost comparisons against self-consistency isolate only the first.

What does help is model heterogeneity. At equal numbers of calls, mixed-model debate beats single-model debate.

Before adding agents, run the baseline: the same model, the same budget, and a vote.

The full paper is attached below.
question: Has a multi-agent setup in your own work ever beaten a plain majority vote at the same cost?
